oneLiner: MAX 2 g/day in cirrhosis (any Child-Pugh class) and active alcohol use — first-line analgesic in liver disease but dose-restricted. AVOID in acute liver failure.
mechanism: Hepatic metabolism via glucuronidation, sulfation, and small fraction via CYP2E1 to NAPQI (the toxic metabolite). In cirrhosis or chronic alcohol use, glutathione stores are depleted and CYP2E1 may be induced, increasing NAPQI accumulation. Standard 4 g/day adult dose risks hepatotoxicity in these settings.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce to max 2-3 g/day; safer than NSAIDs (which carry GI bleed + renal risk in cirrhosis).
guidance.notes: Avoid combination paracetamol-opioid products that risk inadvertent overdose.

guidance.adjustment: Max 2 g/day; preferred analgesic over NSAIDs and opioids.
guidance.notes: Monitor LFTs at baseline and 1 week, then 3-monthly.

guidance.adjustment: Max 2 g/day with caution; consider 1-2 g/day only in severe disease.

monitoring: Baseline LFTs; repeat 1 week after starting then 3-monthly. Educate patient to avoid concurrent paracetamol-containing OTC products (cough/cold combinations).
acuteFailureGuidance: AVOID — additional paracetamol load worsens injury. Use cautious opioid (fentanyl preferred — no active metabolites, hepatic clearance preserved) at reduced dose.

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Review article: prescribing medications in patients with cirrhosis. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.
Khalid SK et al. Use of analgesics in cirrhosis. Postgrad Med J 2019.

oneLiner: AVOID in cirrhosis — precipitates AKI (hepatorenal syndrome), GI bleeding from varices, and worsens ascites. Risk increases through Child-Pugh classes.
mechanism: Prostaglandin inhibition impairs renal autoregulation — cirrhotic patients depend on prostaglandin-mediated renal perfusion (already reduced by splanchnic vasodilation). NSAIDs precipitate functional renal failure (HRS). Also worsens sodium / water retention (ascites) and impairs platelet function in patients already coagulopathic.

guidance.adjustment: Avoid where possible; short-course only with renal function monitoring.

monitoring: If short-course needed in Class A: creatinine and electrolytes before, day 3, and at end of course.
alternatives: tramadol with caution (50% dose; risk of encephalopathy)

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: Reduce dose and extend interval in moderate-severe cirrhosis — clearance falls 50-75%. Risk of accumulation → respiratory depression, hepatic encephalopathy. Fentanyl preferred for parenteral use.
mechanism: Morphine undergoes hepatic glucuronidation to active morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G, analgesic) and inactive morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G, neurotoxic). In cirrhosis, glucuronidation is relatively preserved but biliary excretion fails — both metabolites accumulate. Renal impairment (common in cirrhosis) compounds accumulation.

guidance.adjustment: Start at 50-75% standard dose; titrate cautiously.
Start at 25-50% standard dose AND extend interval (e.g. q6-8h instead of q4h).
guidance.notes: Monitor sedation, respiratory rate, and signs of encephalopathy.

guidance.adjustment: Start at 25% standard dose with extended interval; consider fentanyl PCA / patch instead (no active metabolites, hepatic clearance preserved).

monitoring: Sedation score, respiratory rate, GCS, signs of hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis, confusion). Naloxone immediately available.
acuteFailureGuidance: Fentanyl is the parenteral opioid of choice (no active metabolites; clearance largely unaffected by liver failure). Avoid morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone.

references.label: Tegeder I et al. Pharmacokinetics of opioids in liver disease. Clin Pharmacokinet 1999.

drug: Benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam, alprazolam, clonazepam vs lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam)
oneLiner: AVOID long-half-life benzos in cirrhosis (precipitate encephalopathy). If essential: LORAZEPAM, OXAZEPAM or TEMAZEPAM (glucuronidated — clearance preserved). Reduce dose by 50%.
mechanism: Diazepam, midazolam, alprazolam, clonazepam undergo hepatic CYP3A oxidation — clearance markedly reduced in cirrhosis with prolonged sedation and risk of hepatic encephalopathy. Lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam are conjugated by glucuronidation only — pathway largely preserved in liver disease.

guidance.adjustment: Use cautiously; prefer glucuronidated agents (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam); halve dose of CYP3A-metabolised benzos.
guidance.notes: Avoid alcohol-withdrawal benzo regimens with long-acting agents — switch to lorazepam-CIWA-Ar.

guidance.adjustment: Lorazepam / oxazepam / temazepam at 50% dose. AVOID diazepam, midazolam, alprazolam, clonazepam.
AVOID all benzodiazepines unless essential. If essential: lorazepam 0.5 mg single doses with neurological monitoring.
guidance.notes: Refractory agitation in hepatic encephalopathy is often treated by addressing the precipitant (lactulose, rifaximin), not sedation.

monitoring: Sedation score, GCS, asterixis, signs of encephalopathy. Avoid in patients with prior encephalopathy.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al. Drug dosage recommendations in patients with chronic liver disease. Rev Esp Enferm Dig 2012.

oneLiner: Compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A): statins ACCEPTABLE and may improve outcomes. Decompensated (Class B/C) or active hepatocellular disease: AVOID. Discontinue if ALT > 3× ULN.
mechanism: Mostly hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4 for simvastatin, atorvastatin; CYP2C9 for fluvastatin; minimal CYP for pravastatin and rosuvastatin). Hepatotoxicity is rare but recognised. Cirrhosis impairs first-pass metabolism — exposures rise.

guidance.adjustment: Standard or reduced starting dose; observational data suggest statins improve hepatic outcomes in compensated cirrhosis.
Use with caution and at reduced dose; benefit-risk highly individualised. Decompensation is a relative contraindication.
guidance.notes: Avoid statins in active hepatocellular injury / decompensation.
Discontinue if started prior to decompensation.

monitoring: Baseline LFTs; recheck 4-12 weeks; then 6-monthly. Discontinue if ALT > 3× ULN persistently.
alternatives: dietary intervention + risk factor modification first-line in decompensated disease

references.label: Bays H et al. An assessment by the Statin Liver Safety Task Force. J Clin Lipidol 2014.

drug: Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
oneLiner: Child-Pugh C: CONTRAINDICATED for ALL DOACs. Class B: avoid rivaroxaban (specifically contraindicated); use apixaban with caution. Cirrhosis raises bleeding risk independent of anticoagulant.
mechanism: Apixaban and rivaroxaban undergo CYP3A4 metabolism — exposure rises in advanced cirrhosis. Dabigatran is renally cleared but cirrhosis often comes with reduced renal function. All DOACs are associated with worsened bleeding in cirrhosis (varices, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, vitamin K deficiency).

guidance.adjustment: All DOACs may be used at standard doses. Bleeding risk slightly higher than non-cirrhotic but acceptable.

RIVAROXABAN CONTRAINDICATED (specific labelling). Apixaban with caution at standard dose; some guidance favours apixaban in this group. Dabigatran avoided due to coexisting renal impairment. Edoxaban not recommended.
guidance.notes: LMWH or warfarin (with careful INR control) often preferred.
Use LMWH; warfarin difficult due to baseline INR derangement.

monitoring: Hb, platelets, coagulation, LFTs, renal function. Variceal surveillance every 1-2 years (per BSG/AASLD). Clinical bleeding endpoints.
alternatives: no anticoagulation if bleeding risk outweighs thrombotic risk

references.label: Northup PG et al. Vascular liver disorders, portal vein thrombosis, and anticoagulation in cirrhosis. AASLD 2020.

oneLiner: Compensated cirrhosis: ACCEPTABLE — observational benefit. Decompensated (Class B/C): AVOID due to lactic acidosis risk, particularly with concomitant renal impairment.
mechanism: Renal excretion (not hepatic metabolism). Cirrhosis itself raises lactate clearance burden (impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate). Combined with cirrhosis-associated renal impairment (HRS, NSAID exposure), lactic acidosis risk rises.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing acceptable; consider continuing — observational data suggest reduced HCC risk and improved survival in compensated cirrhosis.
guidance.notes: Monitor renal function and lactate if any concern.

guidance.adjustment: Caution — reduce dose and consider alternatives if HCC or renal impairment present.
guidance.notes: Lactate measurement if any clinical concern (tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting, drowsiness).
Particularly with acute decompensation, HRS, sepsis, or hypoperfusion.

acuteFailureGuidance: Withhold during any acute illness (sepsis, AKI, contrast exposure, dehydration) regardless of baseline liver status.

references.label: Vilar-Gomez E et al. Long-term metformin use may improve clinical outcomes in diabetic patients with compensated NASH-related cirrhosis. Hepatology 2017.

oneLiner: Inherently hepatotoxic — use with caution in any pre-existing liver disease, avoid in Child-Pugh C unless TB justifies the risk. Monitor LFTs frequently; do NOT confuse asymptomatic ALT rise with hepatitis.
mechanism: Hepatic metabolism by deacetylation and biliary excretion. Potent CYP3A4 inducer (alters many co-prescribed drug levels). Hepatotoxicity rate ~ 1-2% in TB therapy; baseline liver disease raises this several-fold.

guidance.adjustment: Use with intensive baseline + weekly LFT monitoring for first 2 months. Hold at ALT > 5× ULN or ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms.
guidance.notes: Hepatology / TB-specialist input for any DILI.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose; monitor LFTs twice weekly first 2 months. Consider liver-sparing TB regimen (e.g. moxifloxacin + ethambutol + linezolid).
guidance.notes: MDR-TB regimens are an active area of practice change — discuss with TB specialist.

guidance.adjustment: AVOID where possible; use specialist-supervised liver-sparing regimens.
guidance.notes: Decompensation post-rifampicin in cirrhotic TB patients carries high mortality.

monitoring: Baseline LFTs; weekly first month, fortnightly to 8 weeks, monthly thereafter. Hepatitis B/C status at baseline (pre-treatment).

references.label: Saukkonen JJ et al. ATS / IDSA / CDC official statement: hepatotoxicity of antituberculosis therapy. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2006.

oneLiner: FIRST-LINE diuretic in cirrhotic ascites (counters hyperaldosteronism). Standard adult dose 100-400 mg/day with furosemide 40-160 mg/day (5:2 ratio). Monitor K⁺, renal function, sodium.
mechanism: Aldosterone receptor antagonist. Hepatic metabolism to active canrenone. Cirrhotic ascites is driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism; spironolactone directly addresses the mechanism. Dose-limited by hyperkalaemia and renal function.

guidance.adjustment: Start 100 mg/day; titrate to 400 mg/day if needed. Often combined with furosemide 40-160 mg/day (Mascalchi 5:2 ratio).
guidance.notes: Monitor K⁺ and renal function weekly during titration.

guidance.adjustment: Same as Class A — first-line for ascites.
guidance.notes: Anticipate need for combination diuretics; watch for HRS.

guidance.adjustment: Continue at lower dose; HRS / renal failure risk is high — hold if creatinine rising or K⁺ > 5.5.
guidance.notes: Refractory ascites: large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement; TIPS; transplant assessment.

monitoring: K⁺, Na⁺, creatinine, urea — weekly during titration, then 2-4 weekly. Hold if K⁺ > 5.5 mmol/L. Monitor weight loss target ~ 0.5 kg/day (no peripheral oedema) or 1 kg/day (with oedema).
alternatives: furosemide alone (less effective in cirrhotic ascites; risk of intravascular depletion)

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of patients with decompensated cirrhosis. J Hepatol 2018.

drug: Propranolol (and carvedilol) — non-selective beta-blockers for varices
oneLiner: First-line for primary and secondary prevention of variceal bleeding in cirrhosis. Use lowest effective dose; titrate to HR 55-60 bpm. CONSIDER STOPPING in decompensated Class C with refractory ascites / HRS / hypotension.
mechanism: Non-selective β-blockade + α₂ unopposed splanchnic vasoconstriction reduces portal pressure. Hepatic clearance is reduced in cirrhosis — start low.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing for variceal prophylaxis: propranolol 20-40 mg BD titrated to HR 55-60 (max 320 mg/day); or carvedilol 6.25-12.5 mg/day.
Same as Class A; standard for primary / secondary variceal prophylaxis.
Use with caution — STOP if refractory ascites + SBP < 90 mmHg, HRS, or SBP develops. Hold during decompensation; consider band ligation alone.
guidance.notes: 'Window hypothesis': beta-blockers may worsen outcome in very decompensated cirrhosis with refractory ascites.

monitoring: BP, HR, renal function. Look for HRS / hypoperfusion signals.
alternatives: endoscopic variceal band ligation alone (in patients unsuited to beta-blockade)

references.label: Garcia-Tsao G et al. AASLD Practice Guidance: Portal Hypertensive Bleeding in Cirrhosis. Hepatology 2017.

oneLiner: Highly hepatically metabolised (CYP2C9/CYP2C19) with saturable kinetics — small dose changes cause large level changes. Reduce dose 30-50% in Class B/C, monitor FREE phenytoin (albumin-bound; bound fraction falls in cirrhosis).
mechanism: CYP2C9 + CYP2C19 hepatic metabolism; non-linear (Michaelis-Menten) kinetics — small dose increments give large concentration increments near saturation. Albumin-bound (90%); in cirrhosis / hypoalbuminaemia, the free (active) fraction rises and total levels MISREPRESENT toxicity.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing with TDM; check free phenytoin if available, otherwise interpret total level with albumin correction.
guidance.notes: Sheiner-Tozer correction: corrected = measured / (0.2 × albumin g/dL + 0.1). Free phenytoin target 1-2 µg/mL.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce loading dose to 75% and maintenance to 50-75%; use FREE phenytoin levels for monitoring.
guidance.notes: Increased risk of cerebellar / cognitive toxicity at lower total levels.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 30-50% and consider alternative AED (levetiracetam — renal clearance, no hepatic metabolism, no protein binding issues).
guidance.notes: High risk of toxicity at standard dosing.

monitoring: Free phenytoin level (preferred over total in cirrhosis); LFTs; signs of nystagmus, ataxia, drowsiness, hyperammonaemia.
alternatives: levetiracetam (preferred — renal clearance, no protein binding, no CYP interactions)

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: Hepatic CYP3A metabolism — exposure rises sharply in liver dysfunction. Reduce dose 25-50% in Class B; consider 50-75% reduction with intensive TDM in Class C. Common scenario: post-liver-transplant patient with allograft dysfunction.
mechanism: CYP3A4 / CYP3A5 hepatic metabolism, biliary excretion. Narrow therapeutic window (trough 5-15 ng/mL post-transplant; varies by indication and time). In liver dysfunction, clearance falls and exposure rises, increasing nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hyperglycaemia, hyperkalaemia.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing with TDM; consider 25% reduction if persistent above-target troughs.
guidance.notes: CYP3A5 expresser status affects target dose (see PGx record).

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 25-50% and check trough at 3 days; titrate to target.
guidance.notes: Tighter monitoring of nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity (tremor, headache, encephalopathy).

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50-75% with daily TDM during titration. Consider cyclosporine switch in select cases.
guidance.notes: Allograft dysfunction post-transplant requires transplant-hepatology input.

monitoring: Trough levels (whole blood); creatinine; potassium; magnesium; glucose; neurological status. Drug interactions (CYP3A inhibitors / inducers — azoles, macrolides, rifampicin, anticonvulsants).
alternatives: cyclosporine (also CYP3A but different toxicity profile)

references.label: Birdwell KA et al. CPIC Guideline for CYP3A5 Genotype and Tacrolimus Dosing (2015).

oneLiner: AVOID in Child-Pugh B/C — accumulation precipitates seizures and encephalopathy. Class A: 50 mg q12h max; titrate cautiously. Tramadol also has serotonergic activity — caution with SSRIs.
mechanism: CYP2D6 + CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism to active M1 metabolite. Cirrhosis dramatically prolongs half-life (~ 13 h vs 6 h normal). Lowered seizure threshold; serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs / SNRIs.

guidance.adjustment: Start 50 mg q12h; max 100 mg q12h. AVOID combination with paracetamol if total paracetamol exceeds 2 g/day.
AVOID. Use paracetamol ≤ 2 g/day or low-dose fentanyl instead.

guidance.notes: Use fentanyl (preferred parenteral) or paracetamol < 2 g/day.

monitoring: Mental status, seizure activity, signs of serotonin toxicity (with SSRI/SNRI co-use).

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: PREFERRED parenteral opioid in liver disease — no active metabolites; hepatic clearance modestly affected even in advanced disease.
mechanism: CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites. Clearance modestly reduced in cirrhosis but no neurotoxic accumulation (unlike morphine M3G). High protein binding — free fraction rises in hypoalbuminaemia.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing; usual PCA / patch regimens acceptable.
Start at 75% standard dose; titrate cautiously.
guidance.notes: Use IV PCA in preference to patch where titration needed.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50% and extend interval; close sedation / RR monitoring.
guidance.notes: Patches inappropriate for opioid-naive patient in this group.

monitoring: Sedation score, respiratory rate, GCS, signs of encephalopathy.
acuteFailureGuidance: First-line parenteral opioid in acute liver failure.

references.label: Tegeder I et al. Pharmacokinetics of opioids in liver disease. Clin Pharmacokinet 1999.
Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: AVOID in cirrhosis — CYP2D6-dependent conversion to morphine is unpredictable, and the morphine produced accumulates dangerously.
mechanism: Prodrug requiring CYP2D6 conversion to morphine for analgesia. Cirrhosis affects both the conversion and the downstream morphine clearance. CYP2D6 polymorphisms add further unpredictability.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution and at reduced dose if essential.

monitoring: Sedation, respiratory rate, signs of encephalopathy.

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in moderate-severe cirrhosis. CYP3A4/2D6 metabolism with active metabolite (oxymorphone). Prefer fentanyl when parenteral opioid needed.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A4 / CYP2D6 metabolism with active metabolite oxymorphone. Clearance falls 50% in cirrhosis; both parent and metabolite accumulate.

guidance.adjustment: Start at 50-75% standard dose; titrate cautiously.

monitoring: Sedation score, RR, GCS, signs of encephalopathy.

references.label: Tegeder I et al. Clin Pharmacokinet 1999.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — accumulates similarly to morphine; fentanyl preferred.
mechanism: Hepatic glucuronidation to hydromorphone-3-glucuronide (neurotoxic, accumulates in renal impairment). Cirrhosis lowers clearance.
monitoring: Sedation, RR, GCS, asterixis, signs of encephalopathy.

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: Acceptable in Class A/B at reduced dose; CYP3A4-metabolised partial agonist with ceiling on respiratory depression. Use caution in Class C.
mechanism: Partial μ-agonist; CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism to norbuprenorphine. Sublingual route bypasses first-pass. Ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes overdose less dangerous than full agonists.

guidance.notes: Used in opioid use disorder treatment in cirrhotic patients.
LFT rise has been reported with buprenorphine — monitor.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution at reduced dose; specialist input.
guidance.notes: Avoid high-dose sublingual; SL formulations often more stable than IV.

monitoring: LFTs at baseline and 1-3 monthly; sedation, RR.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al. Rev Esp Enferm Dig 2012.

oneLiner: Methadone is well-tolerated in mild-moderate cirrhosis but unpredictable in advanced disease — long half-life, QT prolongation, accumulation risk. Specialist supervision.
mechanism: CYP3A4 / CYP2B6 metabolism; very long, variable half-life (often > 24h); QT-prolonging. Cirrhosis reduces clearance and raises accumulation / cardiotoxicity risk.

guidance.adjustment: Standard initiation by addiction / palliative specialist; baseline ECG.
Reduce dose; slow titration; ECG monitoring.
guidance.notes: QT risk amplified by hypokalaemia (common in cirrhosis with diuretics).

guidance.adjustment: AVOID where possible; specialist supervision essential if continued.
guidance.notes: Accumulation can cause prolonged sedation, fatal arrhythmia.

monitoring: ECG (QTc), electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺), sedation, RR, LFTs.

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: AVOID in any cirrhosis — accumulation of neurotoxic norpethidine causes seizures.
mechanism: Hepatic N-demethylation to norpethidine (neurotoxic, half-life 15-20h; renally excreted). Cirrhosis + renal impairment → seizures, myoclonus, agitation. Largely obsolete.

guidance.notes: Other opioids preferred even at this level.

references.label: Lewis JH, Stine JG. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2013.

oneLiner: AVOID in cirrhosis where possible — CYP3A oxidation impaired, prolonged sedation, precipitates encephalopathy. Use lorazepam if benzo essential.
mechanism: CYP3A4 metabolism. Clearance markedly reduced in cirrhosis with prolonged sedation and risk of encephalopathy.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution at reduced dose; prefer lorazepam.
guidance.notes: If used for procedural sedation, halve dose.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al. Rev Esp Enferm Dig 2012.

oneLiner: Acceptable for ICU sedation and procedures in cirrhosis at modestly reduced infusion rate; rapid offset preserved.
mechanism: Hepatic and extrahepatic conjugation; very high clearance with rapid offset largely preserved even in cirrhosis. Hypotension is the main concern in volume-depleted cirrhotic patients.

guidance.adjustment: Standard induction and infusion doses; titrate to effect.
Reduce induction dose 25%; cautious infusion titration.
Reduce dose; very cautious titration; lower infusion rates.

monitoring: BP, HR, SpO2, depth of sedation; lactate / triglycerides for prolonged infusion (propofol infusion syndrome).

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al. Rev Esp Enferm Dig 2012.

oneLiner: Reduce infusion dose in cirrhosis — hepatic clearance impaired; useful alternative to benzos for ICU sedation.
mechanism: Selective α2 agonist; hepatic glucuronidation and CYP metabolism. Clearance falls progressively through Child-Pugh classes.

guidance.notes: Useful for ICU sedation avoiding delirium.

references.label: FDA label / SmPC for dexmedetomidine; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in any cirrhosis; AVOID in Class C — risk of encephalopathy and prolonged sedation.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A metabolism. Z-drugs share benzo-like GABA-A modulation; same encephalopathy risks in cirrhosis.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50% (e.g. zopiclone 3.75 mg, zolpidem 5 mg); short course only.

references.label: BNF Z-drug cautions; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Useful for analgesia / sedation in cirrhosis — primarily extrahepatic clearance preserved at procedural doses. Limit prolonged infusions (hepatotoxicity with chronic use).
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A/2B6 metabolism to norketamine (active). High clearance preserved. Chronic infusions (> several days) associated with cholestatic LFT rise.

guidance.adjustment: Standard procedural and sub-anaesthetic analgesia doses.

monitoring: BP, HR, dissociation; LFTs if prolonged use.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al. Rev Esp Enferm Dig 2012.

oneLiner: Amoxicillin alone: standard dosing in cirrhosis. Co-amoxiclav: well-recognised cause of cholestatic DILI — use cautiously.
mechanism: Renal excretion (parent compound). Clavulanate carries a small but consistent risk of cholestatic hepatitis (delayed, idiosyncratic), more prominent in older patients and prolonged courses.

guidance.adjustment: Amoxicillin standard dosing. Co-amoxiclav with baseline + interval LFT monitoring.
Same; weigh benefit of co-amoxiclav vs alternative.
Same; co-amoxiclav DILI may be poorly tolerated.
guidance.notes: Use narrower-spectrum or alternative if appropriate.

monitoring: LFTs if prolonged course or DILI suspicion.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on Drug-Induced Liver Injury (2019).

oneLiner: Standard dosing in cirrhosis; first-line for SBP prophylaxis / treatment. Reduce dose only if combined hepatic + severe renal impairment.
mechanism: Mixed hepatobiliary and renal excretion. Useful in cirrhosis for SBP, sepsis. Risk of biliary pseudolithiasis with prolonged courses.

guidance.notes: Watch biliary pseudolithiasis with prolonged courses.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose only if combined hepatic + severe renal impairment.

monitoring: Renal function, LFTs, signs of biliary obstruction with prolonged use.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on decompensated cirrhosis 2018.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in severe cirrhosis — hepatic metabolism impaired, risk of accumulation and neurotoxicity.
mechanism: Hepatic oxidation and conjugation. Accumulation in cirrhosis can cause peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy.

references.label: BNF / SmPC metronidazole liver disease section.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Caution with concurrent nephrotoxic agents (cirrhotic patients are more nephrotoxin-sensitive).
mechanism: Renal excretion. Hepatic clearance negligible. Cirrhotic patients are predisposed to AKI which then affects vancomycin clearance.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing with TDM; closer renal monitoring.
guidance.notes: Cirrhotic patients more prone to AKI.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing with TDM; adjust per renal function.

references.label: IDSA / ASHP vancomycin TDM 2020.

oneLiner: Standard dosing in cirrhosis (non-CYP hepatic metabolism); use with caution given thrombocytopenia and lactic acidosis risk in advanced disease.
mechanism: Non-enzymatic oxidation; no CYP involvement. Toxicities (myelosuppression, neuropathy, lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome) of concern in cirrhotics with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperlactataemia.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose with caution; monitor lactate.
guidance.notes: Lactic acidosis precipitating factor in decompensated patient.

monitoring: FBC weekly; lactate; serotonergic drug interactions.

references.label: FDA linezolid label; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in Class B/C — hepatically metabolised, accumulation risk; also recognised cause of cholestatic injury.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism with biliary excretion. Accumulates in cirrhosis. Idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatitis reported.

guidance.notes: C. difficile risk in any cirrhotic patient.

alternatives: depends on indication; macrolide or metronidazole for anaerobes

references.label: BNF clindamycin liver disease section.

oneLiner: Inherently hepatotoxic — combined with rifampicin in TB therapy, hepatitis risk multiplied. Avoid in Class C unless TB justifies; intensive LFT monitoring throughout.
mechanism: Hepatic N-acetylation; rate determined by NAT2 polymorphism. Hepatotoxicity well-recognised (idiosyncratic), amplified by rifampicin, alcohol use, age, baseline liver disease.

guidance.adjustment: Standard 5 mg/kg/day with intensive LFT monitoring; co-prescribe pyridoxine 25 mg/day.
guidance.notes: Stop if ALT > 5× ULN or > 3× ULN with symptoms.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose; closer monitoring; TB-specialist supervision.

monitoring: LFTs at baseline, weekly first month then fortnightly; symptoms of hepatitis; peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine).

references.label: Saukkonen JJ et al. ATS / IDSA / CDC 2006.

oneLiner: Highly hepatotoxic — usually omitted or replaced in Class B/C cirrhosis; specialist TB input.
mechanism: Hepatic hydrolysis to pyrazinoic acid; intrinsic hepatotoxin. Risk highest in first 2 months of therapy.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing only with intensive monitoring.

monitoring: LFTs intensively first 2 months; uric acid.

references.label: Saukkonen JJ et al. ATS / IDSA / CDC 2006.

oneLiner: Renally cleared, minimal hepatic effect — useful in liver-sparing TB regimens. Monitor visual function.
mechanism: Mostly renal excretion; modest hepatic metabolism. Optic neuritis is the dose-limiting toxicity.

guidance.notes: Visual acuity / colour vision at baseline.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; useful in liver-sparing regimens.
guidance.notes: Adjust per renal function (cirrhotic AKI common).

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; adjust per renal function.

monitoring: Visual acuity / colour vision monthly; renal function.

references.label: WHO consolidated guidelines on TB treatment.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — recognised cause of hepatocellular and cholestatic DILI; CYP inhibitor (many interactions).
mechanism: Renal excretion of parent. CYP2C9 / CYP3A4 inhibitor — drug-drug interactions important in polypharmacy. Idiosyncratic hepatitis at higher doses.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; lowest effective dose; stop on rising ALT.

references.label: EASL Drug-Induced Liver Injury guidelines 2019.

oneLiner: Reduce maintenance dose 50% in Child-Pugh A/B (per label); AVOID in Class C — frequent and severe hepatotoxicity.
mechanism: Extensive hepatic CYP2C19 / CYP3A4 metabolism. Hepatotoxicity common; potent CYP inhibitor.

guidance.adjustment: Standard loading; maintenance dose halved per SmPC.
Standard loading; maintenance halved with TDM.

references.label: EMA / FDA voriconazole label.

oneLiner: Avoid in active liver disease — CYP3A4-metabolised with prominent hepatotoxicity; potent CYP3A inhibitor.
mechanism: CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibition. Idiosyncratic hepatitis. Negative inotrope — caution in heart failure.

references.label: BNF / SmPC itraconazole.

oneLiner: Renally cleared; no hepatic dose adjustment. First-line for chronic hepatitis B; useful in HIV + HBV co-infection.
mechanism: Renal excretion. Used to treat HBV / HIV; particularly important in cirrhotic HBV patients (rapid hepatic decompensation if interrupted).

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose adjusted for renal function.
Standard dose; do not interrupt in HBV cirrhosis (flare and decompensation risk).

monitoring: Creatinine, phosphate, urinalysis; HBV DNA / HBeAg as appropriate.

references.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on HBV (2017).

oneLiner: Avoid in moderate-severe hepatic impairment — extensive CYP metabolism, hepatotoxicity, lipid effects.
mechanism: CYP2B6 / CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism with active metabolites. Hepatotoxicity prominent; neuropsychiatric effects.

references.label: EACS guidelines on ART in liver disease.

oneLiner: Standard dose in Class A/B; avoid in Class C (limited data). Preferred over efavirenz in cirrhotic HIV patients.
mechanism: UGT1A1 / CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Hepatotoxicity uncommon; integrase inhibitor with high barrier to resistance.

guidance.notes: Preferred over efavirenz in liver disease.

alternatives: raltegravir (similar mechanism; alternative in severe liver disease)

references.label: EMA / FDA dolutegravir label; EACS guidelines.

oneLiner: Standard dosing in any cirrhosis — UGT1A1 metabolism with minimal CYP involvement, useful in advanced liver disease.
mechanism: Hepatic UGT1A1 glucuronidation; minimal CYP. Lower hepatotoxicity signal than older agents.

guidance.notes: Useful in severe hepatic impairment per EACS.

references.label: EACS guidelines; EMA raltegravir label.

oneLiner: Avoid in Class B/C — extensive hepatic metabolism, hyperbilirubinaemia (UGT1A1 inhibition) confounds monitoring.
mechanism: CYP3A4 metabolism; potent UGT1A1 inhibitor (causing benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that complicates assessment in cirrhotic patients).

references.label: EACS guidelines.

oneLiner: Use with caution in any liver disease — hepatotoxicity, CYP3A4 inhibition. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.
mechanism: Ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor — extensive CYP3A metabolism. Hepatotoxicity and many interactions.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; reduce dose only if specifically indicated.

references.label: EACS guidelines.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Cirrhotic AKI requires reduced dose; narrow therapeutic window.
mechanism: Renal excretion. Cirrhotic patients are more prone to AKI and electrolyte derangement (hypokalaemia from diuretics) which amplify digoxin toxicity.

guidance.notes: Watch K⁺ in patients on diuretics.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; closer renal / K⁺ monitoring.
Reduce dose for AKI; specialist input.

monitoring: Digoxin level; renal function; K⁺, Mg²⁺.

references.label: BNF digoxin.

oneLiner: Avoid in active liver disease — inherently hepatotoxic with steatohepatitis. Use only where benefit clearly outweighs risk.
mechanism: Extensive hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism; deposition causes steatohepatitis indistinguishable from NASH. Very long half-life (weeks).

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; intensive LFT monitoring.

monitoring: LFTs at baseline and 6-monthly; TFTs; chest imaging.

references.label: BNF amiodarone; EASL DILI 2019.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — high hepatic first-pass extraction; clearance markedly reduced.
mechanism: Extensive CYP2D6 hepatic first-pass metabolism. Bioavailability rises in cirrhosis. CYP2D6 polymorphism adds variability.

guidance.adjustment: Start at 50% standard dose; titrate to HR/BP.
Start at 25-50% dose with slow titration.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: First-line non-selective β + α-blocker for variceal prophylaxis. Start low; titrate to HR/BP. Hold during decompensation.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP2D6 / CYP2C9 metabolism. Non-selective beta + alpha blockade reduces portal pressure more than propranolol at lower doses.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution — stop if refractory ascites, HRS, SBP develops, or hypotension.

references.label: Garcia-Tsao G et al. AASLD 2017.

oneLiner: Mixed renal/hepatic clearance — reduce dose modestly in advanced cirrhosis.
mechanism: Roughly 50:50 hepatic and renal clearance. Cardioselective β1 blocker — not first-choice for variceal prophylaxis (no portal-pressure benefit beyond β1).

guidance.notes: Not for variceal prophylaxis (use carvedilol / propranolol).

references.label: BNF bisoprolol.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Not first-line for variceal prophylaxis (cardioselective).
mechanism: Renal excretion. Cardioselective β1 blocker.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose adjusted for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function.

references.label: BNF atenolol.

oneLiner: Compensated cirrhosis (Class A): acceptable, may improve outcomes. Decompensated: avoid.
mechanism: CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Hepatotoxicity rare but recognised.

guidance.adjustment: Standard or reduced starting dose with LFT monitoring.
Use with caution; reduced dose; weigh benefit vs risk.

references.label: Bays H et al. J Clin Lipidol 2014.

oneLiner: Avoid in active liver disease — CYP3A4 substrate with many interactions and dose-dependent hepatotoxicity at high dose.
mechanism: CYP3A4-dependent; high-dose simvastatin (80 mg) associated with myopathy and higher DILI risk.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; reduce dose; prefer alternative statin.

references.label: Bays H et al. J Clin Lipidol 2014.

oneLiner: Minimal CYP metabolism — preferred statin in compensated cirrhosis; still avoid in decompensated disease.
mechanism: Minimal CYP2C9 hepatic metabolism; predominantly biliary excretion of unchanged drug. Lower interaction profile.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; preferred over CYP-metabolised statins.

references.label: Bays H et al. J Clin Lipidol 2014.

oneLiner: Minimal hepatic CYP metabolism — preferred statin in compensated cirrhosis.
mechanism: Hepatic uptake by OATP1B1; minimal CYP metabolism; renal excretion of metabolites. Lower DILI signal.

references.label: Bays H et al. J Clin Lipidol 2014.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — limited data in advanced liver disease; minimal hepatic metabolism but biliary excretion.
mechanism: Glucuronidation in intestine and liver; biliary excretion of metabolite. Effect on enterohepatic cholesterol absorption.

references.label: EMA / FDA ezetimibe label.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Avoid in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites (HRS risk; worsens renal perfusion).
mechanism: ACE inhibition reduces angiotensin-mediated renal perfusion that cirrhotic patients depend on. Risk of AKI / HRS / hyperkalaemia.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; close renal function and K⁺ monitoring.

references.label: EASL decompensated cirrhosis guidelines 2018.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis (CYP2C9 metabolism). Avoid in decompensated disease — HRS / hyperkalaemia risk.
mechanism: CYP2C9 / CYP3A4 conversion to active metabolite. Cirrhosis reduces this conversion, lowering antihypertensive effect; AT1 blockade still affects renal perfusion.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; reduced dose; renal / K⁺ monitoring.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — extensive hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism, half-life prolonged.
mechanism: CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Half-life lengthens markedly in cirrhosis.

references.label: BNF amlodipine; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — extensive CYP3A4 metabolism; potent CYP3A inhibitor.
mechanism: CYP3A4 metabolism and inhibition. Many interactions (statins, tacrolimus, midazolam).

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — high hepatic first-pass extraction; bioavailability greatly increased.
mechanism: Extensive CYP3A4 first-pass metabolism. Cirrhosis raises bioavailability several-fold.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — hepatic N-acetylation impaired; acetylator status affects exposure. Drug-induced lupus risk.
mechanism: Hepatic N-acetylation (NAT2-polymorphic). Slow acetylators have higher exposure. Drug-induced lupus and idiosyncratic hepatitis recognised.

references.label: BNF hydralazine.

oneLiner: Difficult to use in advanced cirrhosis — baseline INR derangement, lower factor synthesis, narrow therapeutic window. LMWH usually preferred in Class B/C.
mechanism: Inhibits vitamin-K-dependent factor synthesis (II, VII, IX, X). Cirrhosis already lowers these factors; baseline INR derangement makes monitoring unreliable.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dosing with careful INR monitoring.
Use with caution; INR control challenging; consider LMWH alternative.

guidance.notes: Baseline INR not reflective of bleeding risk.

references.label: Northup PG et al. AASLD 2020.

oneLiner: Preferred anticoagulant in moderate-severe cirrhosis. Standard prophylactic / treatment doses; adjust for renal function and weight.
mechanism: Predominantly renal excretion. Cirrhotic patients often have reduced antithrombin; clinical bleeding risk depends on platelets, varices, renal function.

guidance.notes: VTE prophylaxis indicated in hospitalised cirrhotic patients.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; adjust per renal function; consider anti-Xa monitoring.
Use with caution; anti-Xa monitoring; specialist haematology input.

monitoring: Renal function, platelets, anti-Xa (advanced disease), Hb.

references.label: Northup PG et al. AASLD 2020.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — adds GI / variceal bleeding risk. Avoid in active variceal bleeding or thrombocytopenia.
mechanism: Irreversible COX-1 inhibition. Bleeding risk amplified by cirrhotic varices and thrombocytopenia.

guidance.adjustment: Use if clear cardiovascular indication; weigh against bleeding risk.
AVOID with significant thrombocytopenia or known varices.

references.label: AASLD / EASL antiplatelet in cirrhosis guidance.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — CYP2C19-dependent prodrug activation may be impaired; bleeding risk amplified.
mechanism: CYP2C19 prodrug to active metabolite. Cirrhosis may reduce activation efficiency; bleeding risk from coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis; hepatic metabolism impaired with risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia. Avoid in Class C.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP2C9 metabolism. Cirrhosis prolongs half-life with risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia (impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis adds risk).

guidance.adjustment: Start at low dose; titrate cautiously.

references.label: BNF gliclazide; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: No dose adjustment in hepatic impairment — minimal hepatic metabolism, biliary excretion of unchanged drug. Useful in cirrhotic diabetes.
mechanism: Predominantly biliary excretion of unchanged drug. Minimal hepatic metabolism. Low hypoglycaemia risk.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; clinical data limited in severe disease.

references.label: EMA / FDA linagliptin label.

oneLiner: Standard dose in cirrhosis; mainly renal excretion. Useful where insulin not appropriate.
mechanism: Renal excretion of unchanged drug. Minimal hepatic metabolism.

guidance.adjustment: Standard 100 mg/day; adjust for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function.

references.label: EMA / FDA sitagliptin label.

oneLiner: Standard dose in Class A/B; avoid in Class C — limited data, ketoacidosis and volume-depletion risks compound cirrhotic physiology.
mechanism: Hepatic glucuronidation, modest CYP. Renal glucose excretion mechanism. Volume depletion and euglycaemic DKA risks.

guidance.adjustment: Use with caution; lower dose; monitor volume.

monitoring: Renal function, ketones if unwell, volume status.

references.label: EMA / FDA empagliflozin label.

oneLiner: Standard dose in mild-moderate hepatic impairment; limited data in Class C. Useful where weight loss desired (NASH).
mechanism: Peptide degraded by endogenous proteases; not significantly hepatically metabolised. Improves NASH in trials; pancreatitis risk noted.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; monitor LFTs and pancreatitis.

references.label: EMA / FDA liraglutide / semaglutide labels; NASH trials.

oneLiner: PREFERRED glucose-lowering therapy in advanced liver disease. Reduce dose — hepatic gluconeogenesis impaired, hypoglycaemia risk rises.
mechanism: Hepatic and renal clearance of insulin. Advanced cirrhosis reduces clearance and impairs gluconeogenesis — both raise hypoglycaemia risk.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce total daily dose; closer monitoring.
Reduce dose substantially; intensive BM monitoring; specialist diabetes input.

monitoring: BM 4-6×/day; HbA1c interpretation limited by anaemia.

references.label: EASD / ADA cirrhosis diabetes management.

oneLiner: AVOID in active liver disease or family history of hepatic disorder — intrinsic hepatotoxicity with potentially fatal idiosyncratic injury, particularly in children and POLG mutations.
mechanism: Hepatic beta-oxidation; depletes carnitine; idiosyncratic mitochondrial hepatotoxicity (highest risk young children, POLG mutations). Hyperammonaemia common.

guidance.adjustment: Use only if essential; intensive LFT monitoring.

monitoring: LFTs intensively first 6 months; ammonia if symptomatic; valproate levels.
acuteFailureGuidance: AVOID — valproate is itself a cause of acute liver failure.

references.label: EMA valproate / POLG warning; EASL DILI 2019.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — extensive hepatic metabolism, idiosyncratic hepatitis and cholestasis recognised. Reduce dose.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism to active 10,11-epoxide; potent auto-inducer. Idiosyncratic hepatitis; hypersensitivity (DRESS).

guidance.adjustment: Reduce starting dose; slow titration with LFT monitoring.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.; EASL DILI 2019.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50-75% in Class B/C — hepatic glucuronidation impaired. Useful AED in cirrhosis but slow titration essential (rash risk).
mechanism: Hepatic UGT glucuronidation. Cirrhosis reduces clearance.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50-75% per SmPC; slow titration; specialist input.

references.label: EMA / FDA lamotrigine label.

oneLiner: PREFERRED AED in cirrhosis — minimal hepatic metabolism; renal excretion. No protein binding issues.
mechanism: Mostly renal excretion of unchanged drug; minor enzymatic hydrolysis (not CYP). No protein binding interactions.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; adjust for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function; reduce for AKI.

references.label: EMA / FDA levetiracetam label.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in moderate-severe cirrhosis — partially hepatic metabolism with reduced clearance.
mechanism: Renal excretion of parent (~70%); 30% hepatic metabolism. Clearance reduced in cirrhosis.

references.label: BNF topiramate; Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Renally excreted — no hepatic dose adjustment. Adjust for renal function; sedation common in cirrhotic patient.
mechanism: Renal excretion of unchanged drug. No hepatic metabolism.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose adjusted for renal function.
Standard dose adjusted for renal function; watch sedation.
Reduce dose; adjust for AKI; sedation worsens encephalopathy.

references.label: BNF gabapentin.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in Class A; avoid in Class B/C — extensive hepatic metabolism, risk of QT prolongation and hyponatraemia.
mechanism: CYP-mediated hepatic metabolism. Cirrhosis prolongs half-life. SSRI hyponatraemia compounds cirrhotic dilutional hyponatraemia.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in cirrhosis; max 20 mg/day citalopram (10 mg escitalopram). QT prolongation dose-dependent.
mechanism: CYP2C19 / CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Cirrhosis prolongs half-life. QT prolongation dose-related.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose with QT monitoring; max as per SmPC.
Reduce dose 50%; max 20 mg citalopram / 10 mg escitalopram.

references.label: EMA citalopram / escitalopram safety updates.

oneLiner: AVOID in cirrhosis — anticholinergic effects (constipation precipitates encephalopathy), sedation, cardiotoxicity in overdose.
mechanism: CYP2D6 / CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism with active nortriptyline. Anticholinergic and sodium-channel effects.

guidance.adjustment: Use only at very low dose; titrate cautiously.

references.label: BNF amitriptyline.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 30-50% in cirrhosis; useful for sleep, appetite, mood in advanced liver disease.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP1A2 / CYP3A4 metabolism. Clearance reduced 30-40% in cirrhosis. Sedation, appetite stimulation helpful in cachectic cirrhotic patient.
alternatives: sertraline at low dose for non-cachectic

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — CYP1A2 metabolism. Sedation may worsen encephalopathy; weight gain / dyslipidaemia in NASH patients.
mechanism: CYP1A2 / UGT hepatic metabolism. Significant metabolic and weight effects undesirable in NASH.
alternatives: haloperidol low dose for acute agitation

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 25-50% in cirrhosis — CYP3A4 metabolism. Useful low-dose for sleep but sedation can precipitate encephalopathy.
mechanism: CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Sedation, hypotension; QT prolongation.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50%; sedation can precipitate encephalopathy.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Use at reduced dose in cirrhosis — hepatic metabolism; less sedation than other antipsychotics but QT and EPS risks.
mechanism: CYP3A4 / CYP2D6 hepatic metabolism. Less sedation, less hypotension than other antipsychotics — often used for delirium.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50%; low dose (0.5-1 mg) for delirium.

references.label: BNF haloperidol.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Caution with diuretic-treated cirrhotic patient (volume depletion raises lithium toxicity risk).
mechanism: Renal excretion. Cirrhotic patients on diuretics are prone to volume depletion, raising lithium levels.

guidance.adjustment: TDM; watch volume status with diuretics.
Use with caution; intensive TDM; HRS / AKI raises toxicity risk.

references.label: BNF lithium.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — hepatic CYP2C19 metabolism. Avoid unnecessary prolonged PPI (SBP risk).
mechanism: Hepatic CYP2C19 metabolism. Half-life prolonged in cirrhosis. Prolonged PPI use raises spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) risk in ascites.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose; review need; PPI raises SBP risk.

references.label: EASL decompensated cirrhosis guidelines 2018; AASLD SBP guidance.

oneLiner: Reduce max daily dose to 8 mg in moderate-severe hepatic impairment per SmPC — hepatic metabolism, QT prolongation.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP3A4 / CYP1A2 / CYP2D6 metabolism. Half-life doubles in severe hepatic impairment.

references.label: EMA / FDA ondansetron label.

oneLiner: Reduce dose 50% in cirrhosis — hepatic metabolism. EPS / NMS risk.
mechanism: Hepatic CYP2D6 metabolism. Half-life prolonged in cirrhosis with raised EPS / NMS risk.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50%; short course; EPS risk.

references.label: BNF metoclopramide; EMA short-course indication update.

oneLiner: FIRST-LINE for hepatic encephalopathy — non-absorbable disaccharide titrated to 2-3 soft stools/day. Safe across all Child-Pugh classes.
mechanism: Non-absorbed disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria producing acidification and trapping of ammonia as ammonium for faecal excretion. Reduces nitrogen load and modulates gut flora.

guidance.adjustment: Used prophylactically post-HE; titrate to 2-3 soft stools/day.
First-line for HE; titrate to stool target.
First-line for HE; titrate to stool target; over-dosing causes electrolyte derangement / volume loss.

monitoring: Stool frequency / consistency; mental status; electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺).
acuteFailureGuidance: Used for HE in ALF — evidence weaker than chronic cirrhosis but standard of care.

references.label: AASLD / EASL HE guidance 2014.

oneLiner: Standard dose in any cirrhosis — minimally absorbed; second-line / adjunct for recurrent HE.
mechanism: Non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic acting in the gut; reduces ammonia-producing bacteria. <0.5% systemic absorption.

guidance.adjustment: Standard 550 mg BD for recurrent HE prophylaxis.

references.label: AASLD / EASL HE guidance 2014; Bass NM et al. NEJM 2010.

oneLiner: AVOID in any cirrhosis — intrinsic hepatotoxicity with chronic fibrotic injury.
mechanism: Hepatic accumulation with chronic dosing causes fibrosis and cirrhosis. Particularly risky in pre-existing liver disease, NAFLD, alcohol use.

guidance.adjustment: AVOID; consider only with hepatology MDT.

monitoring: If used: LFTs, FBC, renal function; baseline + interval Fibroscan.

references.label: BSR / EULAR methotrexate hepatic monitoring guidance.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — recognised hepatotoxicity (cholestatic, nodular regenerative hyperplasia). TPMT genotype-dosed.
mechanism: Prodrug to 6-mercaptopurine; TPMT-dependent inactivation. Hepatotoxicity (cholestasis, NRH, sinusoidal injury) recognised.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose; TPMT testing; intensive LFT monitoring.

references.label: BSR / EASL DILI 2019.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — CYP3A4 metabolism, accumulation, nephrotoxicity; many drug interactions.
mechanism: Extensive CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Cirrhosis raises exposure. Nephrotoxic, hypertensive — issues in cirrhotic patient with HRS predisposition.

guidance.adjustment: Reduce dose 50%; daily TDM during titration; specialist input.

monitoring: Trough levels, creatinine, BP, electrolytes, LFTs.

references.label: Periáñez-Párraga L et al.

oneLiner: Standard dose in moderate hepatic impairment; limited data in Class C. Useful steroid-sparing immunosuppressant.
mechanism: Hepatic glucuronidation; biliary and renal excretion. Cirrhosis modestly affects clearance.

references.label: EMA / FDA mycophenolate label.

oneLiner: Standard dose in cirrhosis — prednisolone is the active form (prednisone requires hepatic conversion that may be impaired). Use prednisolone preferentially.
mechanism: Prednisolone is the active drug. Prednisone is a prodrug requiring hepatic 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase conversion — may be reduced in cirrhosis.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; use prednisolone in preference to prednisone.
Standard dose; monitor glucose, electrolytes, infection.
Standard dose; intensive monitoring; sodium/volume effects worsen ascites.

references.label: EASL severe alcoholic hepatitis guidelines.

oneLiner: Standard dose in cirrhosis — fully active without hepatic conversion; minimal mineralocorticoid effect (less ascites worsening).
mechanism: Long-acting glucocorticoid; no mineralocorticoid activity. Hepatic metabolism but full activity does not depend on conversion.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; intensive monitoring of glucose / infection.

references.label: BNF dexamethasone.

oneLiner: Use with caution in moderate hepatic impairment; avoid in severe — CYP3A4 / CYP2D6 metabolism, hypotension.
mechanism: CYP3A4 / CYP2D6 hepatic metabolism. Alpha-1 blocker — hypotension risk in cirrhotic patient with reduced systemic vascular resistance.

references.label: EMA tamsulosin label.

oneLiner: Reduce dose in cirrhosis — extensive CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism; consider lower starting dose.
mechanism: CYP3A4 hepatic metabolism. Hypotension risk in cirrhotic patient; many drug interactions.

guidance.adjustment: Start at low dose (25 mg sildenafil); titrate.

references.label: EMA sildenafil / tadalafil labels.

oneLiner: Standard dose in cirrhosis — modest hepatic metabolism; widely used in cirrhotic rheumatology patients.
mechanism: Hepatic and renal clearance. Hepatotoxicity uncommon. Retinal toxicity is the dose-limiting feature.

references.label: BSR hydroxychloroquine guidance.

oneLiner: Use with caution in cirrhosis — hepatic acetylation, idiosyncratic hepatitis, marrow suppression.
mechanism: Cleaved in colon to sulfapyridine + 5-ASA. Sulfapyridine hepatic acetylation. Idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity recognised.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose with LFT / FBC monitoring.

references.label: BSR sulfasalazine guidance.

oneLiner: Renally cleared — no hepatic dose adjustment. Reduce dose for AKI in cirrhotic patient.
mechanism: Renal excretion of unchanged drug. Crystalluria with high IV doses and dehydration.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose adjusted for renal function.
Standard dose; adjust for renal function.
Adjust for AKI; hydration with IV use.

references.label: BNF aciclovir.

oneLiner: Reduce dose modestly in severe cirrhosis — mixed renal/hepatic clearance. Used for SBP prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients.
mechanism: Roughly 50% renal, 50% hepatic / biliary clearance. CYP1A2 inhibitor. Tendinopathy, dysglycaemia, QT prolongation risks.

guidance.adjustment: Standard dose; useful for SBP prophylaxis.
Reduce dose for AKI; LFT / glucose monitoring; QT.

references.label: EASL decompensated cirrhosis guidelines 2018.
